questions.knowledge_point: Identifying a Possible Curve Given Its Arc Length As an Integral
questions.problem: The length of a curve $y=f(x)$ is given by ${\int }_{0}^{1}\sqrt{2+4{x}^{2}-4x}\,\text{d}x.$ Which of the following could be  an equation for this curve?
questions.worked_solution:
The arc length of a curve $y=f(x)$ between $x=a$ and $x=b$ can be found using the formula

$$
L={\int }_{a}^{b}\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

We're given that 

$$
L={\int }_{0}^{1}\sqrt{2+4{x}^{2}-4x}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Comparing the above with the arc length formula, we see that we must have

$$
[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}=4{x}^{2}-4x+1=(2x-1)^{2}\,⟹\,{f}^{′}(x)=\pm (2x-1).
$$

Integrating the above equation with respect to $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\pm \int (2x-1)\text{ d}x \\  & =\pm ({x}^{2}-x)+C.\end{aligned}
$$

From the given options, the only one that has the required form is $y={x}^{2}-x+4.$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Arc Length of a Smooth Curve Using the Arc Length Formula
questions.problem: Compute the arc length of $y=\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}$ for $x\in [\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2},1].$
questions.worked_solution:
The arc length of a curve $y=f(x)$ between $x=a$ and $x=b$ can be found using the formula

$$
L={\int }_{a}^{b}\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

In our case, $f(x)=\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}},$ $a=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$ and $b=1.$

First, we find the derivative of $f(x):$

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=-\frac{x}{\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}}
$$

Now, let's compute $\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}} & =\sqrt{1+{(-\frac{x}{\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+\frac{{x}^{2}}{1-{x}^{2}}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{1-{x}^{2}+{x}^{2}}{1-{x}^{2}}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{1}{1-{x}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}}$ to the formula for the arc length, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{\sqrt{2}/2}^{1}\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{\sqrt{2}/2}^{1}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =(\operatorname{arcsin}⁡x){|}_{\sqrt{2}/2}^{1} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}-\frac{\pi }{4} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
The arc length of a curve $y=f(x)$ between $x=a$ and $x=b$ can be found using the formula

$$
L={\int }_{a}^{b}\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}\,\text{d}x.

We're given that 

$$
L={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{1+{sin}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Comparing the above with the arc length formula, we see that we must have

$$
[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}={sin}^{2}⁡x\,⟹\,{f}^{′}(x)=\pm \operatorname{sin}⁡x.
$$

Integrating the above equation with respect to $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\pm \int \operatorname{sin}⁡x\text{ d}x \\  & =\pm \operatorname{cos}⁡x+C.\end{aligned}

$$

$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Arc Length of a Smooth Curve Using the Arc Length Formula
questions.worked_solution:
The arc length of a curve $y=f(x)$ between $x=a$ and $x=b$ can be found using the formula

$$
L={\int }_{a}^{b}\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

In our case, $f(x)=\frac{2}{3}(x+2)^{3/2},$ $a=1,$ and $b=6.$

First, we find the derivative of $f(x):$

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=\frac{2}{3}\cdot \frac{3}{2}(x+2)^{1/2}=\sqrt{x+2}
$$

Now, let's compute $\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}} & =\sqrt{1+{[\sqrt{x+2}]}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+(x+2)} \\  & =\sqrt{x+3}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}=\sqrt{x+3}$ to the formula for the arc length, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{1}^{6}\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{6}\sqrt{x+3}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={(\frac{2}{3}(x+3)^{3/2})|}_{1}^{6} \\  & =[\frac{2}{3}(6+3)^{3/2}]-[\frac{2}{3}(1+3)^{3/2}] \\  & =\frac{54}{3}-\frac{16}{3} \\  & =\frac{38}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$
